title: Six-Axis Industrial Robot
subtitle: Six joints, a harmonic drive in every axis and a gripper that repeats to a tenth of a millimetre
summary: An industrial robot is a chain of six controlled joints. Each joint has a motor, a gearbox that multiplies its torque, a brake and an encoder that reports its angle. The controller combines those six angles into one position in space, so the tool can follow a path, hold a part, or weld a seam with the same accuracy every cycle.

parts.name: Base and Foot
parts.short: Bolts the robot to the floor
parts.detail: A stiff cast base carries the first joint and spreads the arm's overturning load into the foundation. Its bolts are pre-tensioned so the base never rocks.

parts.name: Axis 1 Drive
parts.short: Rotates the whole arm about the base
parts.detail: A servo motor drives a reduction gearbox that turns the turret. Axis 1 has to move the mass of the entire arm, so its gear ratio is high.

parts.name: Turret
parts.short: Carries the shoulder and the upper arm
parts.detail: The rotating column between axis 1 and axis 2. It contains the shoulder bearing and the cable path from the base into the arm.

parts.name: Axis 2 Shoulder
parts.short: Raises and lowers the upper arm
parts.detail: A horizontal joint with a large servo and gearbox on the shoulder. Its brake must hold the arm's weight when power is removed.

parts.name: Upper Arm
parts.short: The main link from shoulder to elbow
parts.detail: A hollow cast or welded link. It is stiff in bending but light, because every kilogram here becomes torque the shoulder motor must carry.

parts.name: Axis 3 Elbow
parts.short: Bends the forearm
parts.detail: The elbow joint shares the arm's reach between two links. Its motor and gearbox sit on the joint axis to keep the moving mass balanced.

parts.name: Forearm
parts.short: The second link, out to the wrist
parts.detail: A slimmer link that carries the wrist motors and the tool. Its low mass is what lets the robot accelerate quickly at full reach.

parts.name: Axis 4 Roll
parts.short: Rolls the wrist around the forearm
parts.detail: Axis 4 rotates the wrist along the forearm's axis. Its motor is often mounted back in the arm and drives through a shaft or belt.

parts.name: Wrist and Axis 5
parts.short: Pitches the tool up and down
parts.detail: A compact two-axis wrist. Axis 5 bends the tool, and the fork transfers the load into the roll bearing of axis 4.

parts.name: Axis 6 Flange
parts.short: Spins the tool on its own axis
parts.detail: The final joint turns the mounting flange. Its hollow shaft often carries air and wiring for the gripper.

parts.name: Tool Flange
parts.short: The standard mounting face for tools
parts.detail: A precision disc with a bolt circle and locating feature. Any tool that matches the flange can be fitted and calibrated.

parts.name: Parallel Gripper
parts.short: Two jaws that hold the workpiece
parts.detail: A pneumatic cylinder closes two fingers on the part. The pads spread the grip load and are changed for different materials.

parts.name: Air Hoses
parts.short: Supply the gripper cylinder
parts.detail: Two flexible lines carry compressed air to the gripper. They are routed with a service loop so they do not stretch at full wrist rotation.

parts.name: Cable Harness
parts.short: Power and signals along the arm
parts.detail: Motor cables and encoder signals run from the base to each joint. The harness is clamped to the links so it flexes instead of chafing.

parts.name: Counterbalance Spring
parts.short: Helps the shoulder lift the arm
parts.detail: A gas spring or mechanical spring offsets part of the arm's weight. It lets a smaller shoulder motor hold the arm steady.

parts.name: Joint Brakes
parts.short: Hold each axis when power is off
parts.detail: Spring-applied, electrically released brakes sit on the motor shafts. They keep the arm from falling during a stop or power failure.

parts.name: Encoders
parts.short: Report every joint angle
parts.detail: Each axis carries an absolute encoder. The controller needs the exact angle of all six joints to know where the tool is.

parts.name: Control Cabinet
parts.short: The computer and drives that move the arm
parts.detail: The cabinet holds the robot controller, servo drives and safety circuits. It converts a programmed path into six motor commands.

parts.name: Teach Pendant
parts.short: The hand-held programming terminal
parts.detail: A screen and jog buttons used to move the robot and record points. The dead-man switch must be held for the arm to move in teach mode.

parts.name: Nameplate
parts.short: Model, payload and serial number
parts.detail: The plate gives the robot's rated payload, reach and serial number, which set the safe working envelope.

steps.title: Six joints, one point
steps.body: Each joint adds one rotation. The controller multiplies the six angles through the link lengths to find the tool's position and orientation.

steps.title: Motors are too fast, so gears slow them
steps.body: A servo spins quickly with little torque. A harmonic or cycloidal drive reduces the speed and multiplies the torque, while adding almost no backlash.

steps.title: The arm must not fall
steps.body: Each axis has a spring-applied brake. When power drops, the brakes clamp the motor shafts and hold the arm where it is.

steps.title: The tool repeats, not just reaches
steps.body: Encoders and a stiff structure let the same program return to the same point cycle after cycle. Repeatability, not just reach, is what makes a robot useful.

quiz.prompt: Tap the joint that rotates the whole arm on its base.
Tap the part that holds the workpiece.
Tap the part that reports each joint's angle.
Why does each axis need a gearbox?
choices: To make the motor spin faster
To trade motor speed for torque
quiz.explain: Servo motors are fast and weak; the gearbox reduces speed and multiplies torque.

quiz.prompt: What happens when power is removed?
quiz.explain: The brakes are spring-applied and electrically released, so they hold the arm when power is lost.
